comments.content:
Kaggle is becoming something like Formula 1. You need skills and talent, but financial resources are also playing an increasingly large role. It's neither good nor bad, it's reality.

It's a bit disappointing that the vast majority of competitions with an accessible amount of data are trading competitions (with poorly formulated problem statements, for example, predicting some index a year ahead), many of which end completely randomly (and most of the winners don't even publish their solutions).

replies.content: It has always been this way. Maybe 15 years ago, even before XGBoost existed, you could solve a ton of tabular competitions on a basic laptop using just linear regression. But with the start of the DL era and the surge of computer vision competitions, access to powerful hardware has always been an advantage—and even more so now in the LLM era. Overall, this is a competitive sport, and it always has a financial component. Some people solve ARC Prizes just to secure fat new funding rounds for their startups, and that's okay. Anything that isn’t forbidden is allowed. As for publishing solutions, especially in financial trading competitions, everything is fair game. I’ve also stopped writing write-ups and sharing code. I just don't want LLMs to train on it and help participants in future similar competitions ;)

replies.content:
No, Kaggle has no "fell off the last few years". There are plenty community competitions, playground competitions — anyone can grow here!

For me featured competitions is when you compete with the best in the field. In 2026, being the best in LLM-related problems obviously requires some resources — it's a prerequisite. Any problem that need SFT+ requires some GPUs. Hosts literally invest a lot of money and expect some ROI! It's also up to them to decide what data could we use.

Out of my 8 gold medals only 2 required some substantial compute (>= $1000; but there were teams placed higher, that spent less!) and 6 were 100% possible with free Kaggle GPUs — I do not see anything unfair here. And I missed like many competitions that were also very easily winnable with no compute at all, just read the writeups, its mostly just v smart engineering and data research.

And regarding this competition.

Being able to come up with an algorithm that is able to differentiate between (same family) LLMs would be so cool. For example in that case, some form of an audit could be performed in order to verify that providers indeed give us the models we paid for. It is very important. So if someone spend just $5.000 or so and solves this, then its a huge W for the community. I dont see any reasons to seriously whine about potential progress of some teams and moreover I'd be happy to see this solutions, even when I cant afford myself to spend that much $$$ on data etc

replies.content:
I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

You are a bit naive in your assumptions about the nature of Kaggle. This isn't an entertainment platform. And competitions ranks are not ment to be a pure display of skill (there is a strong correlation tho)

The primary purpose of Kaggle isn't to provide fair or equal competitions for the sake of it. It is to create an environment for people, companies, organizations and businesses to find effective solutions to real problems at hand.

Kaggle will try to make competitions fair where reasonable, but at the end of the day if the problem happens to be solvable / simplifyable with the employment of extra GPUs, well, okay. There are a lot of competitions on Kaggle and other platforms where resources do not convert to an advantage. And if you wanna learn — late submissions are always open, notebooks are shared. There is a lot of room for learning

I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

@samson8 For a Competition Host in Kaggle, do you think which Team below is more valuable to them if the Team end up become the final winner of the Competition they Host ?

Team A: Won by scaling up enormous computing resources and data volume that no body can match, focus on using standard publicly available data , idea and algorithm.

Team B: Won with unique idea and specialize but limited data that are way less compare to Team A

As a Competition Host with all the money to scale up their infrastructure and data volume, what Team A can value add to the Host compare to Team B?

The problem today is not about fairness, we don't talk about fairness in a Competition as long as the rules is not been broken. But for the benefit of the Competition Host, some way to make everybody use the same compute resources is in the best interest of the Competition Host, and what happen currently where some Team can win based on Compute Resource alone, beating out Team with much better idea is Not a good trend.

replies.rawMarkdown:
No, Kaggle has no "fell off the last few years". There are **plenty** community competitions, playground competitions — anyone can grow here!

For me featured competitions is when you **compete** with the best in the field. In 2026, being the best in LLM-related problems obviously **requires** *some* resources — it's a prerequisite. Any problem that need SFT+ requires some GPUs. Hosts literally invest a lot of money and expect some ROI! It's also up to them to decide what data could we use.

Out of my 8 gold medals only 2 required some substantial compute (>= $1000; but there were teams placed higher, that spent less!) and 6 were 100% possible with free Kaggle GPUs — I do not see anything unfair here. And I missed like many competitions that were also very easily winnable with no compute at all, just read the writeups, its mostly just v smart engineering and data research.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

And regarding this competition.

Being able to come up with an algorithm that is able to differentiate between (same family) LLMs would be so cool. For example in that case, some form of an audit could be performed in order to verify that providers indeed give us the models we paid for. It is very important. So if someone spend just $5.000 or so and solves this, then its a huge W for the community. I dont see any reasons to seriously whine about potential progress of some teams and moreover I'd be happy to see this solutions, even when I cant afford myself to spend that much $$$ on data etc

replies.content:
I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

You are a bit naive in your assumptions about the nature of Kaggle. This isn't an entertainment platform. And competitions ranks are not ment to be a pure display of skill (there is a strong correlation tho)

The primary purpose of Kaggle isn't to provide fair or equal competitions for the sake of it. It is to create an environment for people, companies, organizations and businesses to find effective solutions to real problems at hand.

Kaggle will try to make competitions fair where reasonable, but at the end of the day if the problem happens to be solvable / simplifyable with the employment of extra GPUs, well, okay. There are a lot of competitions on Kaggle and other platforms where resources do not convert to an advantage. And if you wanna learn — late submissions are always open, notebooks are shared. There is a lot of room for learning

I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

Some data on this question: we tried adding the public 18-model corpus (licensed rows only, ~15k texts) to a simple char+word TF-IDF + LinearSVC, and scored with GroupKFold by prompt on competition texts only.

  • competition data only: 0.326
  • + 850 external rows that are already single paragraphs: 0.308
  • + 14,911 external rows flattened to one paragraph: 0.279

We saw the same direction with a stronger TF-IDF and with frozen Qwen3-8B embeddings. Our main suspect is the mismatch: competition texts have 0% line breaks and 0% bold, while 94% / 60% of the external answers do, and the external median length is 174 words vs 101. So "more data" may matter, but only if it looks like the host's data.

Details and code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/mizuno0522/model-fingerprints-punctuation-external-data

replies.content: There are differences in architecture and post-training. As much as we want an actual universal function approximator, architecture really impedes learning (at least with gradient descent via backpropogation). Pretraining-wise, pretty much everyone trains on some filtered version of common crawl + wikipedia + reddit (if they're rich). Differences in the RL pipeline employed and architecture are where the behavioral traits come in.

Any competent model, maybe even a copy of the top public work retrained with those labels was a top silver solution or more. To me this seems directly against the rules on ever competition but its never actually enforced so a sudden enforcement without an annoucement would be unfair too.

replies.content: I don’t think that’s the issue. I think it’s about what the solution intends: is it to train a base model on data that none of us can compete with, against those putting forward the challenge? replies.content:
I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

Some data on this question: we tried adding the public 18-model corpus (licensed rows only, ~15k texts) to a simple char+word TF-IDF + LinearSVC, and scored with GroupKFold by prompt on competition texts only.

  • competition data only: 0.326
  • + 850 external rows that are already single paragraphs: 0.308
  • + 14,911 external rows flattened to one paragraph: 0.279

We saw the same direction with a stronger TF-IDF and with frozen Qwen3-8B embeddings. Our main suspect is the mismatch: competition texts have 0% line breaks and 0% bold, while 94% / 60% of the external answers do, and the external median length is 174 words vs 101. So "more data" may matter, but only if it looks like the host's data.

Details and code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/mizuno0522/model-fingerprints-punctuation-external-data

replies.content:
No, Kaggle has no "fell off the last few years". There are plenty community competitions, playground competitions — anyone can grow here!

For me featured competitions is when you compete with the best in the field. In 2026, being the best in LLM-related problems obviously requires some resources — it's a prerequisite. Any problem that need SFT+ requires some GPUs. Hosts literally invest a lot of money and expect some ROI! It's also up to them to decide what data could we use.

Out of my 8 gold medals only 2 required some substantial compute (>= $1000; but there were teams placed higher, that spent less!) and 6 were 100% possible with free Kaggle GPUs — I do not see anything unfair here. And I missed like many competitions that were also very easily winnable with no compute at all, just read the writeups, its mostly just v smart engineering and data research.

And regarding this competition.

Being able to come up with an algorithm that is able to differentiate between (same family) LLMs would be so cool. For example in that case, some form of an audit could be performed in order to verify that providers indeed give us the models we paid for. It is very important. So if someone spend just $5.000 or so and solves this, then its a huge W for the community. I dont see any reasons to seriously whine about potential progress of some teams and moreover I'd be happy to see this solutions, even when I cant afford myself to spend that much $$$ on data etc

replies.content:
I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

comments.content:
Some data on this question: we tried adding the public 18-model corpus (licensed rows only, ~15k texts) to a simple char+word TF-IDF + LinearSVC, and scored with GroupKFold by prompt on competition texts only.

  • competition data only: 0.326
  • + 850 external rows that are already single paragraphs: 0.308
  • + 14,911 external rows flattened to one paragraph: 0.279

We saw the same direction with a stronger TF-IDF and with frozen Qwen3-8B embeddings. Our main suspect is the mismatch: competition texts have 0% line breaks and 0% bold, while 94% / 60% of the external answers do, and the external median length is 174 words vs 101. So "more data" may matter, but only if it looks like the host's data.

Details and code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/mizuno0522/model-fingerprints-punctuation-external-data

replies.content:
No, Kaggle has no "fell off the last few years". There are plenty community competitions, playground competitions — anyone can grow here!

For me featured competitions is when you compete with the best in the field. In 2026, being the best in LLM-related problems obviously requires some resources — it's a prerequisite. Any problem that need SFT+ requires some GPUs. Hosts literally invest a lot of money and expect some ROI! It's also up to them to decide what data could we use.

Out of my 8 gold medals only 2 required some substantial compute (>= $1000; but there were teams placed higher, that spent less!) and 6 were 100% possible with free Kaggle GPUs — I do not see anything unfair here. And I missed like many competitions that were also very easily winnable with no compute at all, just read the writeups, its mostly just v smart engineering and data research.

And regarding this competition.

Being able to come up with an algorithm that is able to differentiate between (same family) LLMs would be so cool. For example in that case, some form of an audit could be performed in order to verify that providers indeed give us the models we paid for. It is very important. So if someone spend just $5.000 or so and solves this, then its a huge W for the community. I dont see any reasons to seriously whine about potential progress of some teams and moreover I'd be happy to see this solutions, even when I cant afford myself to spend that much $$$ on data etc

replies.content:
I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

You are a bit naive in your assumptions about the nature of Kaggle. This isn't an entertainment platform. And competitions ranks are not ment to be a pure display of skill (there is a strong correlation tho)

The primary purpose of Kaggle isn't to provide fair or equal competitions for the sake of it. It is to create an environment for people, companies, organizations and businesses to find effective solutions to real problems at hand.

Kaggle will try to make competitions fair where reasonable, but at the end of the day if the problem happens to be solvable / simplifyable with the employment of extra GPUs, well, okay. There is a lot of room for learning

I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

No, Kaggle has no "fell off the last few years". There are **plenty** community competitions, playground competitions — anyone can grow here!

For me featured competitions is when you **compete** with the best in the field. In 2026, being the best in LLM-related problems obviously **requires** *some* resources — it's a prerequisite. Any problem that need SFT+ requires some GPUs. Hosts literally invest a lot of money and expect some ROI! It's also up to them to decide what data could we use.

Out of my 8 gold medals only 2 required some substantial compute (>= $1000; but there were teams placed higher, that spent less!) and 6 were 100% possible with free Kaggle GPUs — I do not see anything unfair here. And I missed like many competitions that were also very easily winnable with no compute at all, just read the writeups, its mostly just v smart engineering and data research.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

And regarding this competition.

Being able to come up with an algorithm that is able to differentiate between (same family) LLMs would be so cool. For example in that case, some form of an audit could be performed in order to verify that providers indeed give us the models we paid for. It is very important. So if someone spend just $5.000 or so and solves this, then its a huge W for the community. I dont see any reasons to seriously whine about potential progress of some teams and moreover I'd be happy to see this solutions, even when I cant afford myself to spend that much $$$ on data etc

replies.content:
I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness.

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

@samson8 For a Competition Host in Kaggle, do you think which Team below is more valuable to them if the Team end up become the final winner of the Competition they Host ?

Team A: Won by scaling up enormous computing resources and data volume that no body can match, focus on using standard publicly available data , idea and algorithm.

Team B: Won with unique idea and specialize but limited data that are way less compare to Team A

As a Competition Host with all the money to scale up their infrastructure and data volume, what Team A can value add to the Host compare to Team B?

The problem today is not about fairness, we don't talk about fairness in a Competition as long as the rules is not been broken. But for the benefit of the Competition Host, some way to make everybody use the same compute resources is in the best interest of the Competition Host, and what happen currently where some Team can win based on Compute Resource alone, beating out Team with much better idea is Not a good trend.

Some data on this question: we tried adding the public 18-model corpus (licensed rows only, ~15k texts) to a simple char+word TF-IDF + LinearSVC, and scored with GroupKFold by prompt on competition texts only.

- competition data only: 0.326
- + 850 external rows that are already single paragraphs: 0.308
- + 14,911 external rows flattened to one paragraph: 0.279

We saw the same direction with a stronger TF-IDF and with frozen Qwen3-8B embeddings. Our main suspect is the mismatch: competition texts have 0% line breaks and 0% bold, while 94% / 60% of the external answers do, and the external median length is 174 words vs 101. So "more data" may matter, but only if it looks like the host's data.

Details and code: https://www.kaggle.com/code/mizuno0522/model-fingerprints-punctuation-external-data

comments.raw_markdown:
No, Kaggle has no "fell off the last few years". There are **plenty** community competitions, playground competitions — anyone can grow here!

For me featured competitions is when you **compete** with the best in the field. In 2026, being the best in LLM-related problems obviously **requires** *some* resources — it's a prerequisite. Any problem that need SFT+ requires some GPUs. Hosts literally invest a lot of money and expect some ROI! It's also up to them to decide what data could we use.

Out of my 8 gold medals only 2 required some substantial compute (>= $1000; but there were teams placed higher, that spent less!) and 6 were 100% possible with free Kaggle GPUs — I do not see anything unfair here. And I missed like many competitions that were also very easily winnable with no compute at all, just read the writeups, its mostly just v smart engineering and data research.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

And regarding this competition.

Being able to come up with an algorithm that is able to differentiate between (same family) LLMs would be so cool. For example in that case, some form of an audit could be performed in order to verify that providers indeed give us the models we paid for. It is very important. So if someone spend just $5.000 or so and solves this, then its a huge W for the community. I dont see any reasons to seriously whine about potential progress of some teams and moreover I'd be happy to see this solutions, even when I cant afford myself to spend that much $$$ on data etc

I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

You are a bit naive in your assumptions about the nature of Kaggle. This isn't an entertainment platform. And competitions ranks are not ment to be a pure display of skill (there is a strong correlation tho)

The primary purpose of Kaggle isn't to provide fair or equal competitions for the sake of it. It is to create an environment for people, companies, organizations and businesses to find effective solutions to real problems at hand.

Kaggle will try to make competitions fair where reasonable, but at the end of the day if the problem happens to be solvable / simplifyable with the employment of extra GPUs, well, okay. There are a lot of competitions on Kaggle and other platforms where resources do not convert to an advantage. And if you wanna learn — late submissions are always open, notebooks are shared. There is a lot of room for learning

I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it.

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

@samson8 For a Competition Host in Kaggle, do you think which Team below is more valuable to them if the Team end up become the final winner of the Competition they Host ?

Team A: Won by scaling up enormous computing resources and data volume that no body can match, focus on using standard publicly available data , idea and algorithm.

Team B: Won with unique idea and specialize but limited data that are way less compare to Team A

The problem today is not about fairness, we don't talk about fairness in a Competition as long as the rules is not been broken. comments.raw_markdown:
I’m with you for some of this, absolutely it’s the entire point to give the hosts ROI and they should be able to determine what resources are allowed for competition. Playground series are great! My 4 gold medals were also earned with very little monetary investment (less than 100) but I absolutely have to be strategic about what competitions I pick for this, as many (especially the ones that have released over the last 12 months AIMO, arc, and other LLM or CNN comps) are significantly more difficult to compete in without being financially prepared to pay for some GPU.

Where we disagree, I think it’s pretty clear to see that things are getting significantly more expensive to compete at the highest levels for the LLMs and image comps. Obviously that’s not all Kaggle’s fault, as GPUs have gotten much more expensive. But competitions like this where one could gain a huge advantage from say 5k in extra dataset creation seems more pay to play than seems fair? Or ARC where the GPU investment is almost required to get gold. If I recall (and I could totally be wrong no) I think there is a rule in the Kaggle ruleset to ensure that resources used in solutions is at a reasonable level to maintain fairness. 

For me that last part is really why I care, I would be fine with spending a little extra money for a competition that I thought was interesting. But talking about large sums of money is unfair for competitors who might be students or from less gpu rich countries. I think it’s good to continue to have these types of discussions from both sides so that Kaggle can continue to become a better place, my only point here is that comps like AIMO, arc, and this one that will likely require more spending have gotten much more common than basic no resource required competitions.

You are a bit naive in your assumptions about the nature of Kaggle. This isn't an entertainment platform. And competitions ranks are not ment to be a pure display of skill (there is a strong correlation tho)

The primary purpose of Kaggle isn't to provide fair or equal competitions for the sake of it. It is to create an environment for people, companies, organizations and businesses to find effective solutions to real problems at hand.

Kaggle will try to make competitions fair where reasonable, but at the end of the day if the problem happens to be solvable / simplifyable with the employment of extra GPUs, well, okay. There are a lot of competitions on Kaggle and other platforms where resources do not convert to an advantage. And if you wanna learn — late submissions are always open, notebooks are shared. There is a lot of room for learning

comments.author: Cody_Null
comments.raw_markdown:
I actually totally agree with you on virtually everything, I am simply stating that maybe the “fair where reasonable” bar you talk about, has shifted more lately. I think this entire thread is living proof of it. 

Even if we look at the very rules of the competition it allows for this very confusion between you and I. It specifies little to no cost in multiple places all while saying that hosts have the ultimate control on what reasonable is. Truthfully kaggle should probably just clear up the rules one way or the other because clearly they are different. In practice I would think your point is 100% what is actually used, effectively the host decides. But in theory and in the ruleset I see “minimal cost” and “reasonable”, and I have a tough time calling the use of extreme compute or token cost either.

“6. EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS

a. You may use data other than the Competition Data (“External Data”) to develop and test your Submissions. However, you will ensure the External Data is either publicly available and equally accessible to use by all Participants of the Competition for purposes of the competition at no cost to the other Participants, or satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b below. The ability to use External Data under this Section does not limit your other obligations under these Competition Rules, including but not limited to Section 2.8 (Winners Obligations).

b. The use of external data and models is acceptable unless specifically prohibited by the Host. Because of the potential costs or restrictions (e.g., “geo restrictions”) associated with obtaining rights to use external data or certain software and associated tools, their use must be “reasonably accessible to all” and of “minimal cost”. Also, regardless of the cost challenges as they might affect all Participants during the course of the competition, the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered. The Host will employ an assessment of whether or not the following criteria can exclude the use of the particular LLM, data set(s), or tool(s):

Are Participants being excluded from a competition because of the "excessive" costs for access to certain LLMs, external data, or tools that might be used by other Participants. The Host will assess the excessive cost concern by applying a “Reasonableness” standard (the “Reasonableness Standard”). The Reasonableness Standard will be determined and applied by the Host in light of things like cost thresholds and accessibility.

By way of example only, a small subscription charge to use additional elements of a large language model such as Gemini Advanced are acceptable if meeting the Reasonableness Standard of Sec. 8.2. Purchasing a license to use a proprietary dataset that exceeds the cost of a prize in the competition would not be considered reasonable.

comments.author: Chew Kok Wah
comments.raw_markdown:
@samson8  For a Competition Host in Kaggle, do you think which Team below is more valuable to them if the Team end up become the final winner of the Competition they Host ?   

Team A: Won by scaling up enormous computing resources and data volume that no body can match, focus on using standard publicly available data , idea and algorithm.  
  
Team B: Won with unique idea and specialize but limited data that are way less compare to Team A  

As a Competition Host with all the money to scale up their infrastructure and data volume, what Team A can value add to the Host compare to Team B?

The problem today is not about fairness, we don't talk about fairness in a Competition as long as the rules is not been broken. But for the benefit of the Competition Host, some way to make everybody use the same compute resources is in the best interest of the Competition Host, and what happen currently where some Team can win based on Compute Resource alone, beating out Team with much better idea is Not a good trend.

replies.content: I don’t think that’s the issue. I think it’s about what the solution intends: is it to train a base model on data that none of us can compete with, against those putting forward the challenge? I think they are looking for clever, minimal-training solutions that are architecture- and metrics-based, not heavy compute that trains weights for one specific task—the 18 LLM. My solution is being designed to map the pattern signature of any LLM—tell your grandma to work for your aunt by mapping thought to data-output patterns. I am not sure anyone should have that capability, but I need the practice for my Marlu harness.
